stories.title: Families of the Disappeared to meet Pope Leo
stories.summary: The families of the Disappeared are to meet Pope Leo XIV later this week. It is the first papal audience for members of the families of those abducted, murdered and secretly buried by republicans during the Troubles. The trip has been organised by the Belfast-based Wave Trauma Centre, which supports the families. Archbishop Eamon Martin, Catholic Primate of All Ireland, who helped organise the audience, will travel with the group. Fr Joe Gormley, who leads the annual commemoration service for the families, will also take part. "This visit to the Vatican to meet with Pope Leo is hugely significant for the Families on a number of levels," said Sandra Peake of Wave.

stories.title: Jensen Huang discussing Nvidia return with allies - FT
stories.summary: Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia's chief executive, and ‌has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times has reported, citing people familiar with the matter. One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" ⁠of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that the efforts had Mr Huang's support. The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's ‌board ⁠had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment ⁠outside regular business hours. Mr Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy ⁠that raised questions over exports of the company's advanced AI chips to China.

stories.title: Farrell: 'We know all about them, they know all about us'
stories.summary: Andy Farrell says he has full belief his side can topple the world champions on Saturday, when they renew what has become an epic rivalry with South Africa. Twelve months on from a humbling 24-13 defeat at the Aviva, Ireland host the Springboks this weekend in search of revenge. If they achieve that, it could result in another meeting between the pair the following week. Ireland are third in the northern hemisphere section of the Nations Championship heading into the final round of pool games. France top the northern section on 21 points with England and Ireland just behind on 20. With the French expected to be too good for Argentina, and England holding a vastly superior points difference over Ireland, Andy Farrell's side will have to beat the Springboks this weekend, and hope England come up short against New Zealand, in order to get into second place, which would see them face South Africa at Twickenham on Saturday 28 November. The permutations are a sidebar to what has become one of the spiciest rivalries in recent years.

stories.title: Epic Ireland: the extraordinary true tales that shaped our past
stories.summary: We present an extract from Epic Ireland, the new book for younger readers written by Kieran Fanning and illustrated by Alice Guidi. Join master storyteller Kieran Fanning on a sweeping journey across all 32 counties, uncovering the extraordinary true stories that shaped our island's past. From saints like Brigid of Kildare to sinners like William Burke from Tyrone, this is a book of rebels, pirates, soldiers and explorers. Meet Ireland’s first hangwoman, a tennis star who became a murderer, and a slave who fought his way to freedom and became a champion boxer. Wherever you are in Ireland, there’s a fascinating story, person and site to discover! COUNTY CARLOW: When Hunger Became a Crime - the story of Esther Burgess When disease destroyed the potato crop in 1845 , Ireland was plunged into a terrible famine, forcing starving people to do desperate things. Esther Burgess shivered. The trees she was hiding in did little to protect her from the rain that had been falling for the past hour, soaking her light woollen dress. Mud squelched between the toes of her bare feet. But worse than all that was the hunger. It gnawed at her insides like a live animal. Her daughter Mary stood beside her, 15 years old, and also soaked and shivering, but at least she had shoes. She was probably starving too, like her six brothers and sisters at home.

stories.title: Collins in tears at Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction
stories.summary: Phil Collins has been brought to tears after being honoured with an induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. The Genesis drummer and frontman, 75, was among several British acts who were inducted at the ceremony, which was held in Los Angeles on Saturday night. Collins has not performed on stage since 2022, having suffered from health complications including five operations on his knee, and has previously stated he can only walk with assistance. He has also suffered from back and arm injuries throughout his life caused by years of drumming. During the ceremony, he took to the stage slowly using a pair of canes and cried after receiving a huge ovation from the crowd, which included his daughter, actor Lily Collins. Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker inducted Collins and praised him for his success as both a drummer and a hit-making pop singer in the 1980s.

stories.title: UK PM Burnham to confront 'obvious truth' of Brexit costs
stories.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to announce he wants to have a difficult conversation about the "obvious truth" of the costs of Brexit, in order to reset Britain's relationship with the European Union ahead of a summit in Brussels this week. Mr Burnham is aiming for an agreement at Friday's summit on areas such as food and youth mobility, which could help lower costs for consumers in the short term and ease some of the frictions caused by Britain's departure from the bloc in 2020. However, Mr Burnham is also looking for a broader reassessment of the Brexit deal struck by the previous Conservative government, saying he wants to have a conversation about its legacy that others have avoided. "It's like the emperor's new clothes - where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth," Mr Burnham is set to say in a speech on foreign policy in London's financial district, according to advance excerpts from his office. "Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on. The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained." Mr Burnham's willingness to suggest a broad array of options for the longer-term relationship with the EU reopens a debate that upended British politics when Britain voted to leave the bloc in a 2016 referendum.

stories.title: Trading at Grafton Group in line with expectations
stories.summary: The owner of building supply chains Woodies and Chadwicks saw sales grow in the four months to the end of October, despite a continued decline in its British business. In a trading update this morning Dublin-headquartered Grafton Group - which owns a number of DIY and builders' merchants brands across Europe - said average daily like-for-like sales were up 2% between July and October. On the Island of Ireland, revenues were up 6.5%, which it attributed to "favourable market conditions and continued Government investment in housing and infrastructure." Its Iberian business grew by 7.4% in the period, reflecting the integration of an air conditioning equipment supplier - an area which enjoyed strong demand during the summer. However its Great Britain segment saw sales fall by 5.2%, which Grafton Group said reflected an "ongoing weakness in construction activity" as well as subdued demand in for repair and maintenance work as well as housebuilding. In the year-to-date, Grafton said its sales were up 1.2% across the group.

stories.title: Azaz 'more ready for the role' after latest deep-end dip
stories.summary: While the risk may not have come wrapped in the bow of a positive result, Finn Azaz's display in a deep-lying midfield role against Austria left Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson suitably impressed. The Southampton attacking midfielder has occasionally dropped deeper when the Boys in Green have been chasing games late on. His intervention in the famous 3-2 victory over Hungary in Budapest this time last year was one such occasion when unfolding changes elsewhere in the team saw him pushed further back in the closing crescendo. But last month's 2-2 draw against Austria at Aviva Stadium saw him start in one of the deep midfield roles within Ireland's 5-2-2-1 formation. The question going into the Nations League fixture versus the same opponents on Saturday was whether Hallgrimsson would gamble with Azaz in that 'six' position from the start considering the prowess the Austrians possess on home soil. Ultimately, Azaz did line up in that deeper berth alongside Jayson Molumby and despite falling to a 1-0 defeat in Linz, his manager felt the 26-year-old is quickly adapting to the role.

stories.title: Dolly Parton gave U2 old song to finish for new album
stories.summary: U2 have revealed their collaboration with Dolly Parton on the song Torn came about after she declared their songs were "too Irish" for her. The Irish rock band and the late country music star worked together on the track, which appears on U2's latest album, Carnaval De Luz. The single was co-written by the band, Parton and Snow Patrol star Johnny McDaid. It also became Parton’s last ever recording, with the singer dying in August at the age of 80 following a "brief battle with cancer". Speaking on BBC Radio 2’s Tracks Of My Years With Vernon Kay, the band’s frontman Bono explained how they came together. He said: "We were looking for something to unify our album because it would be nice if when the characters in our album could deal with what’s going on in the outside world. It’s a really fractious time that we live in where everyone’s got a point of view and, you know, you’re the enemy if you don’t agree with them. She’s the penicillin for that, isn’t she? She’s the antidote to all that.

stories.title: Domestic economy to grow 3.5% this year - Ibec
stories.summary: The domestic economy will grow by 3.5% this year and 4% in 2027, according to a forecast by employer group Ibec. The organisation said that the number of people in employment was expected to reach 2.9 million next year. It said that, despite the volatility caused by tariffs introduced by the Trump administration and the effect of high energy prices, the economy continued to show "remarkable resilience". It said while there were "some positive movements" in delivery of homes, housing costs for homeowners and renters continue to increase, due to significant undersupply. Recent data from the Central Statistics Office showed rents rose by 7% in the 12 months to October. Ibec chief economist Gerard Brady said: "Looking at our long-term performance, take-home household income has grown by 50% after inflation, the national payroll is up 40%, and domestic business investment has risen by 44% in the past 10 years."

stories.title: Have tech jobs in Ireland gone from boom to bust?
stories.summary: Analysis: Demand for technology jobs in Ireland remains strong yet there are reasons to be wary about its prospects for the future Ireland is widely regarded as the technology hub or Europe. There are currently over 1,380 technology jobs listed on Irish Jobs, more than half in Dublin. Demand for technology jobs in Ireland remains strong, and you can argue that these are boom times for technology in Ireland. Nevertheless, there are reasons to be wary about the prospects for technology jobs in Ireland in the future. Fields like cybersecurity will probably remain vibrant. There are many bad actors prowling the internet, and people who can help keep organisations safe from these threats will be in demand for the foreseeable future. Many other technology jobs involve or are dependent on artificial intelligence. The state of AI and investment in the infrastructure needed to support AI (e.g. data centres) is looking increasingly uncertain. Two issues make the future of AI very hard to predict. First, doubts are growing about the value of AI to organisations. Technology investments are increasingly judged by the return on investment, and the returns on organisations’ investment in AI are often elusive. Six months ago, most forecasts suggested that organisations could become remarkably more efficient and profitable by using AI, but so far, AI has failed to deliver these benefits. Second, there is a growing belief that the AI bubble is not sustainable. In recent years, much of the economic growth seen in many nations has depended substantially on rapid growth in investments in AI, and the possibility that the AI bubble will burst is an increasing concern. AI companies have invested huge amounts of money in infrastructure development and many have outstanding commitments to spend hundreds of billions more. It is not clear how these organisations will ever make enough selling AI-related products and services to pay off these investments. Recent events have thrown an unexpected wrinkle into the future of AI. Nvidia is the most important chipmaker in the AI universe. Their CEO, Jensen Huang, has recently resigned, after revelations of having an affair with a woman who is believed to be working with Chinese intelligence agencies and who may be involved in smuggling advanced chips into China. Nvidia is critically important to AI, providing the advanced chips that are at the heart of this technology and much of the funding for leading AI firms, and events that disrupt this organisation could have a broad negative effect on technology job markets worldwide.

stories.title: McCoy wants to see Meath clubs back where they belong
stories.summary: Shane McCoy says Wolfe Tones want to put Meath club football back at Leinster's top table after securing their place in the provincial semi-final. His side were in cruise control midway through the second half of their clash with An Tóchar of Wicklow, but they were given a scare before the end. A 14-point gap was whittled down to four at the long whistle to set up a meeting with Westmeath kings the Downs in the last four. "We showed a lot of qualities in the first half," said McCoy. "We set a stall at half-time to come out in the second half and kick on a small bit, get the scoreboard ticking over. "We did that to a certain extent and then An Tóchar started getting their purple patch. Seeing the positives or the threats they had there in the second half and the cut-throughs a few times was a little bit concerning.

stories.title: Australian MP leaves hospital after alleged car attack
stories.summary: Helen Haines, the Australian politician who lost her legs after being repeatedly struck by a car in an alleged attack, said she had been discharged from hospital and was now focused on rehabilitation. "I am very pleased to confirm that I have moved into the rehabilitation stage of my recovery, which will continue in Melbourne for the immediate future," Ms Haines said, in her first public statement since the 19 October attack. "This is a really positive moment," she said, adding that she appreciated the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages she had received from people throughout Australia and around the world. "They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing." Ms Haines said that she was "full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred [Hospital] and am receiving in this next stage." Ms Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital after being rammed by a car outside her office in the small town of Wangaratta in the state of Victoria last month.

stories.title: VC funding to Irish SMEs down sharply in Q3 - IVCA
stories.summary: A global retreat by investors saw venture capital funding to Irish SMEs falling to its lowest in a decade in the three months to the end of September. The latest VenturePulse survey from the Irish Venture Capital Association shows €113.8m in VC funding in the quarter - down 45% year-on-year. In the first nine months of the year, it recorded VC funding of €692.2m - down 19% on the same period of 2025. According to the IVCA, just €35.5m in funding in the third quarter came from international VCs - down 76% year-on-year. This retreat reflected Ireland's overdependence on international investors, it said. While there have been a number of Government schemes launched to try to encourage more domestic VC activity, it said this had so far not grown to the extent required.

stories.title: NFL: Smyth shines again but Saints denied victory
stories.summary: Charlie Smyth nailed a 55-yard field goal for New Orleans Saints against Carolina Panthers on Sunday, but Ryan Fitzgerald slotted a last-second 54-yard kick to snatch a 20-17 win for the Panthers at the Caesars Superdome. Last week Co Down man Smyth kicked three field goals as the Saints secured a 23-22 overtime victory over the Cleveland Browns. Smyth was released last August but a fortnight ago the 25-year-old was dramatically recalled by head coach Kellen Moore after being retained on the practice squad. He continued to justify that decision even though the team could not get over the line this time. Chuba Hubbard ran for two touchdowns and Ryan Fitzgerald kicked a 54-yard field goal as time expired as visiting Carolina defeated New Orleans. Hubbard rushed for 92 yards and Bryce Young, who passed for 200 yards, drove the Panthers (4-5) to the winning field goal after Smyth had tied the score with 41 seconds remaining. Carolina ended a three-game losing streak ⁠and are now first in the NFC South. The Kansas City Chiefs recorded a second straight victory with a 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons.

stories.title: Opposition 'lie' putting peacekeepers at risk - McEntee
stories.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs has accused the Opposition of putting Irish troops in Lebanon in danger because of what she called their "lie" that Irish peacekeepers would be disarming Hezbollah if they took part in the EU mission there. Arriving at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, Helen McEntee said: "The Opposition's suggestions are false, and it is a very dangerous narrative to suggest that the Irish Defence Forces will be working with, whether it's the Lebanese Armed Forces or indeed the Israeli Defence Forces. "It is completely false and inaccurate, and I know from speaking to the Defence Forces that it is potentially putting our [troops] in Lebanon at risk. "I would call on the Opposition, and ask them to stop repeating this lie because they are actually putting our soldiers in the south at risk." She said the EU's Lebanon mission, agreed by foreign ministers in October, was "about training, it's about supporting the [Lebanese Armed Forces], it's about supporting them in many different fields, everything from building up their capacity to be able to monitor and to manage and to work effectively on the ground in Lebanon and all of Lebanon. "It's about supporting them on cyber issues. It's about supporting them on many different matters. It is not about disarming Hezbollah. It is about providing the training and the support that we have provided to many other police forces across the world."

stories.title: Baloucoune: 'Kick in the arse' will prepare us for Boks
stories.summary: If the weekend gone by showed us anything, it's that the Nations Championship is bursting with competitive matchups, meaning the gap between wins and losses is never more than a deep breath away. Fiji, who had never won in Dublin, led Ireland for seven minutes in a ropey first half. France avenged their World Cup heartache with a first Parisian win over South Africa since 2005, while Wales recorded a first victory in 73 years against the mighty All Blacks. If nothing else, it is sure to focus the mind for players and coaches as they reach the halfway point of the November test window. Ireland's 42-12 and 43-15 triumphs seem impressive on paper, but as Robert Baloucoune confessed, the trajectory of the performances was a worry. "We knew they wouldn't go away, so yeah, it's probably a bit disappointing from where we left off with Argentina, but we've got a lot more to focus on now for South Africa coming up," he explained. "I definitely felt it out there. It was definitely a physical battle, and probably lost a few of those battles as well. "So it's a bit of a kick in the arse, to be fair, coming into South Africa because we know what they'll bring, and it's definitely something we're going to look at here."

stories.title: Mullins excited for shot at history with 'special' group
stories.summary: He may have just been named Republic of Ireland Men's Under-21 International Player of the Year on Sunday but the individual accolade couldn't be further from Jamie Mullins' mind. Mullins and his Under-21 teammates are looking to make history on Tuesday in Turner's Cross by qualifying for next summer's European Championships for the first time. It won't be an easy feat following a narrow 1-0 loss to Finland on Friday but confidence is still high within a squad that's pulled out some sensational results to get this far. With their journey looking over before it had even began after a 4-0 loss to Andorra a year ago, the side has shown how resilient they are to bounce back and reach the play-offs. Nothing made that clearer than the conditions that the side were forced to play in on Friday away to Finland. A blizzard coincided with kick-off of the match and both the Finnish players in their white kit and the ball slowly became harder to see. Then there was an extended half-time which reached over 50 minutes. While their opposition had exercise bikes to keep warm, the Irish were left with nothing. "I think it was just a mad night. I think they started the game well and then we wrestled back into it and got momentum back. And then the snow happened, which didn't help anybody," he said. "I think they just scored before half-time, and then at half-time itself, we were in there for nearly 45, 50 minutes. So we didn't really know what was going to happen with the game or what was going on.

stories.title: People less able to exit homelessness over cost - charity
stories.summary: Homeless figures are continuing to rise as the "Government isn't taking the actions necessary to reduce it", the Director of Advocacy with Focus Ireland has said. Mike Allen's remarks come after the number of people in emergency accommodation surpassed 18,000 for the first time. The latest figures from the Department of Housing, which includes just under 6,000 children, shows there were 18,065 homeless in September, a rise of 180 compared to August when the figure stood at 17,885. Mr Allen said the figure has "gone up almost every month" since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic. "And what happened is that people have been less able to get out of homelessness. This, Mr Allen said, is happening because the capacity for people to leave homelessness "has declined".

stories.title: England hold off Spain in Madrid thriller
stories.summary: England ended 2026 with an extraordinary 3-2 triumph in world champions Spain's backyard as Thomas Tuchel’s 10 men dug deep to top their Nations League group on a magical night in Madrid. An intense year that included a heartbreaking World Cup semi-final collapse to Argentina and wild bronze-medal win against France concluded with a chaotic victory against adversity akin to the unforgettable last-16 triumph in Mexico. England roared into an unthinkable three-goal lead at the Metropolitano, where Harry Kane’s penalty gave the visitors a deserved half-time lead that they quickly added to as Ezri Konsa and Ben White silenced Spain. But Elliot Anderson’s sending off in the 63rd minute for bringing down Lamine Yamal after Jarell Quansah was caught out put them on the backfoot against the World Cup winners. Mikel Oyarzabal converted the resulting spot-kick and fellow Euro 2024 final goalscorer Nico Williams came off the bench to reduce the deficit as Tuchel’s team attempted to batten down the hatches. England were made to sweat and James Trafford, given the nod in goal ahead of Jordan Pickford, produced some vital saves to help bring Spain’s 43-game unbeaten record to an end.

stories.title: US air travel set to normalise after days of disruption
stories.summary: US air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 11,500 flights affected, but Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy predicted a return to normalcy even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop. Some 2,100 flights nationwide were cancelled and 9,400 were delayed yesterday, according to aviation data site FlightAware. Airlines on Saturday had cancelled nearly 6,700 US flights and delayed more than 9,100. About 28% of JetBlue flights and 20% of American Airlines flights were cancelled, with United Airlines, Southwest and Delta reporting cancellations of 3% to 5% of their flights. The outlook for the next day was better, with just 88 cancellations today as of 8.28pm Eastern time (1.28am Irish time), FlightAware reported. Mr Duffy said on ABC's "This Week" programme that there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent in the matter, but the cause remained unclear.

stories.summary: Thurles Sarsfields manager Pádraic Maher admitted he was psychologically preparing for a penalty shootout when substitute Robbie Stapleton swung over the winning score in the game's final play against Inagh-Kilnamona in today's semi-final epic in Ennis. Tied at 0-18 apiece at full-time on an afternoon where there was rarely more than a couple of points between the sides, Thurles Sarsfields dug out a win in extra-time, with Stapleton proving the decisive figure. The attacker, who was only introduced for extra-time, hit three of their five points in the additional 20 minutes to edge out the Clare champions. Maher, a six-time All-Star as a player and three-time All-Ireland winner, was captain for Sarsfields' only Munster title back in 2012. As manager, he led them to their first Tipp crown in nine years last month and now they're back in a Munster decider for the first time since 2012, after four successive provincial semi-final losses between 2014 and 2017. "They absolutely emptied themselves there today. Gave everything. The boys that came off the sideline added to the game massively and none more so than Robbie at the end. "It was unbelievable stuff from the whole group. We said coming down on the bus, 'look lads, just give everything you have and we'll see where that leaves us.'

stories.title: Tanker steering problem caused New Orleans ship collision
stories.summary: The asphalt tanker vessel that struck a docked cruise boat in the Mississippi River at New Orleans last week experienced a steering problem in which its rudder was stuck in one position, US transportation safety officials said. The American Cruise Lines passenger vessel American Heritage, with 190 people aboard, capsized at the dock, though no one was killed in the collision. The Atlantic Asphalt tanker was headed upriver when it experienced a "steering casualty" in which its rudder stayed in a starboard position and the vessel veered toward the river's east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum told a news conference in New Orleans. NTSB officials said they do not know what caused the steering problem. Issues under investigation include whether the tanker's anchors were deployed and, if so, at what depth, as well as interviews with crew members and passengers, officials said. Interviews with the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt are scheduled over the next week, they said.

stories.summary: An investigation is under way into the death of a woman whose body was found in Co Offaly. The woman, who was aged in her 20s, was found in an outbuilding on a property in Shinrone. Her body was removed to Midland Regional Hospital Tullamore where a post-mortem examination will take place. The property is a stud farm on the outskirts of Shinrone on the R491. It is understood that the woman was not related to the owners of the property. Local Fianna Fáil Councillor Peter Ormond said everyone in Shinrone was stunned to learn of the incident.

stories.title: Man held after allegedly pulling fake gun on bus driver
stories.summary: A man has been arrested after he allegedly used an imitation firearm and threatened the driver of a bus travelling from Dublin Airport to Cork. The coach, with around a dozen people on board, had left Dublin Airport in the early hours of Saturday morning. As the bus travelled close to Kilworth on the M8 motorway in north Cork, the man is alleged to have pulled an imitation firearm on the driver and made a number of threats. The bus was stopped at the M8 toll plaza at Watergrasshill in Cork and gardaí were contacted. The man has since been charged and is due before Fermoy District Court this morning. The imitation firearm was seized by gardaí and will undergo a ballistic and technical examination.

stories.title: Mixed reaction from NI politicians over Tánaiste's letter
stories.summary: Political leaders in Northern Ireland have given a mixed reaction to an approach from Tánaiste Simon Harris to discuss common ground for Irish reunification. The Fine Gael leader wrote to all political leaders across the island in recent days to seek their views on Irish unity and to share his party's "blueprint" for reunification, with projections it could cost up to €25 billion a year. The party's proposals also include a new junior minister for North-South relations in a dedicated unit within the Department of the Taoiseach and the establishment of a dedicated sovereign wealth fund to deal with the potential costs of the transition. The Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows accused the Tánaiste of "indulging in fairy-tale politics" and that his party had "no interest in a republican invitation to commit political suicide". "There is nothing to be gained from pretending everything would be sweetness and light in your new 'nirvana'. The exercise upon which you have embarked upon is destabilising, unhelpful and potentially dangerous. I would urge you to face reality and devote your energies to building trust," wrote Mr Burrows in response to Mr Harris. The DUP leader Gavin Robinson was also sceptical of the Wicklow TD's correspondence.

stories.title: CUH staff 'fearful' of meetings amid recording concerns
stories.summary: The Chief Executive of the Health Service Executive has claimed staff at Cork University Hospital are fearful of attending meetings amid concerns they might be recorded. Anne O'Connor was speaking as controversy grows around the facility after its CEO Jennifer Kearney warned the HSE, in a letter leaked to the media, how a shortfall of around 1,000 staff meant the hospital would not be safe going into winter. "What worries me probably the most at the minute is the number of staff that I speak to in the hospital who are really very upset about what is going on, who are fearful of going to meetings because they fear they may be recorded. That [applies to] staff within the hospital and staff from outside the hospital going into meetings," she said. "So, we have reached a point where people are just not working together effectively and my ask of everybody is that we get into open and transparent conversations," she added. Seventy patients waited on trolleys on Monday at CUH while earlier this month nine clinical directors at CUH wrote to Taoiseach Micheál Martin about ongoing staffing issues. However, Ms O'Connor dismissed the need for an independent assessment of staff needs at CUH, despite senior clinicians at the hospital calling on the Taoiseach for one.

stories.title: McIlroy wins record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title
stories.summary: Rory McIlroy edged out Eugenio Chacarra to claim a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title with a second-place finish at the DP World Tour Championship, where Tyrrell Hatton sealed a five-shot victory. Spaniard Chacarra had held a slender 533.93-point lead over Masters champion McIlroy going into the season finale at Jumeirah Golf Estates. McIlroy, though, overturned that deficit after a blemish-free fourth round of 67 saw him finish on 10-under-par, on his own in second, to take a fifth successive Race to Dubai crown, matching Colin Montgomerie's record of eight Order of Merit titles. Chacarra had needed to win the tournament to make sure he fended off McIlroy, as well as potentially several other big hitters in the chasing pack. However, a final round of 69, which featured six birdies but also three bogeys either side of the turn, saw him come up just short at eight under in a tie for third, with other scores in the final groups also going McIlroy’s way. Englishman Hatton secured his first DP World Tour Championship title at 15 under, pulling clear following his closing round of 66, which saw him take third place in the overall Race to Dubai standings.
